options: `useCallback([])` freezes the `selectedId` from the first render, so every element it builds keeps that stale comparison; `extraData` only forces a re-render, which re-reads the same frozen value.
`extraData={selectedId}` is missing: `FlatList` is a `PureComponent`, so it skips the render and keeps returning the elements it already produced.
`getItemLayout` is missing, so the list never re-measures a cell whose selected style changed and keeps drawing it at the old geometry.
`Row` needs `React.memo` with a comparator on `selected`, because the default comparison treats a changed boolean as equal.
mcqs.explanation: The bug is a stale closure one level above `FlatList`: `useCallback` with an empty dependency array keeps the first render's `selectedId` forever, so every later render builds `selected: item.id === <first value>` and no row can ever match, while the header - rendered from current state - keeps updating (https://react.dev/reference/react/useCallback). The strongest distractor is option 1, because the rule it states is real: `FlatList` is a `PureComponent`, and a value that affects rows but lives outside `data` must arrive through `extraData` when `renderItem` has a stable reference (https://reactnative.dev/docs/flatlist). But `extraData` is only a re-render marker: it makes the list render again and the render still reads the frozen variable, so the rows stay unselected - that is precisely why the two fixes are not interchangeable. Putting `selectedId` in the dependency array changes `renderItem`'s identity, which already re-renders the list; `extraData={selectedId}` then becomes a cheap defensive extra rather than the fix. Option 3 inverts `memo`'s contract: the default comparison is `Object.is` per prop, so a changed boolean does re-render - the row simply never receives a new element to compare. Option 2 confuses layout measurement with re-rendering.

options: `document` is missing only because the engine has no browser shell, but React Native emulates the DOM over native views, so the grid rule and `<div>` would work once that access is guarded.
The bundle is compiled to Swift and Kotlin, so the failing lines come from a pre-compiled web build, and `document` access belongs in a native module instead.

Core components map to real platform views (`<View>` becomes a `UIView` on iOS and a `ViewGroup` on Android), so there is no DOM and no CSS: no `document`, no `div`, no grid, and sizes are density-independent numbers.
`<div>` is aliased to `<View>` for portability, so only `document` has to be replaced, and the inline style object is the part that keeps working unchanged.
mcqs.explanation: Each core component is a host component that becomes a real native view - `View` maps to `UIView`/`ViewGroup`, `Text` to `UILabel`/`TextView` - and layout is computed by Yoga's flexbox subset, so a React Native app has no DOM, no cascade, no selectors and no `rem`; `document` does not exist on the JS side and `1rem` is not a valid size (https://reactnative.dev/docs/components-and-apis, https://reactnative.dev/docs/layout-props). The strongest distractor is option 0: it half-explains the error correctly (no browser shell) and then bridges to the DOM-emulation myth, but nothing emulates `document` on top of native views - the opposite exists, `react-native-web`, which renders React Native components to the DOM and is a different target. Option 1 reverses the toolchain: the app ships a JavaScript bundle executed by the runtime, and JSX is not compiled into Swift or Kotlin. Option 3 invents an alias table; an unknown host component is not substituted for `View`, and the inline style object only keeps working for properties that exist in React Native.

mcqs.question: A team upgrades to a React Native release where the New Architecture is the default, rebuilds both platforms and retires their last legacy native module. Cold start on the reference low-end Android device is 2.9s, unchanged from 2.8s before, but scrolling and a chart are visibly smoother. What is the correct reading?
options: The migration did not take effect: `newArchEnabled` has to be true and the app rebuilt, otherwise the legacy bridge still runs underneath and only the JavaScript side changed.
Serialization was not their startup bottleneck: the architecture enables capabilities, and the guidance says an app may need refactoring before it gains, so startup needs its own profile.
The benefits require rewriting the app's own components as TurboModules or Fabric components in C++, which this team has not done, so startup stays on the old path.
Fabric commits on the UI thread, so the first launch after an upgrade pays a migration cost and the improvement appears from the second launch onwards.
mcqs.explanation: The official guidance is explicit that enabling the New Architecture "may not immediately improve the performance or user experience", that code may need refactoring to leverage capabilities like synchronous layout effects or concurrent features, and that thanks to JSI removing serialization, "data serialization may not have been a bottleneck" for a given app - so a flat startup number next to a smoother renderer is a normal, expected combination, and startup has to be profiled as its own problem (https://reactnative.dev/architecture/landing-page). The strongest distractor is option 0, because it is the first thing anyone would check and it sounds actionable: if the flag were off, no JSI, Fabric or TurboModules work would happen at all. The premise already rules it out - the release defaults to it and the last legacy module is gone - and the smoother scroll and chart are evidence the new renderer is live, so the flag cannot be the explanation for one metric staying flat. Option 2 confuses app code with native code: your own components stay JavaScript, and only your own native modules and view managers need the JSI/TurboModule or Fabric equivalent. Option 3 invents a warm-up rule; cold start is measured on a fresh install or a rebooted device every time, and a second-launch-only gain is not what the migration promises.

mcqs.question: A team iterates in Expo Go. They install a barcode-scanning library that ships native code and is not part of the Expo Go client, and importing it throws at runtime. What is the correct move?
options: Eject to a bare React Native project: native libraries cannot be used in a project created with Expo, so the `ios/` and `android/` folders have to be owned and maintained by hand.
Run `npx expo prebuild` and stay in Expo Go: prebuild adds the newly installed native module to the Expo Go client on the next start.
Mock the native module during development and link the real one only for store builds, because native behavior cannot be exercised in a debug build.
Create a development build: install `expo-dev-client`, rebuild with `npx expo run:android|ios` or `eas build`, and keep the same project, config plugins and build profiles.
mcqs.explanation: Expo Go is a sandbox with a fixed set of native modules, so a library outside that set cannot run there; a development build is your own version of Expo Go, compiled with the native libraries you actually use plus the dev tooling, which is why it replaces Expo Go as soon as a native dependency appears (https://docs.expo.dev/develop/development-builds/introduction/). The strongest distractor is option 0, the classic eject myth: an Expo app is a React Native app, and needing a native library is a limit of the Expo Go binary, not of the toolchain - the honest cost is one rebuild of your own client, which is cheaper than taking over two native projects. Option 1 confuses `prebuild` with installing into Expo Go: prebuild generates the native projects from the app config (CNG), and it cannot modify the Expo Go app already installed from the store. Option 2 hides the exact behavior under test - the point of a development build is that native code runs in debug, against your JS, on a device.

mcqs.question: CI produces a signed `app-release.apk` and Play Console refuses it for a new app release. What does Play expect instead, and what happens to signing?
options: A universal APK: Play splits it per device at download time, so an APK and a bundle end up producing the same optimized result.
Upload the bundle unsigned: Play signs the bundle and the generated APKs, so an upload key is only needed if you also upload APKs to a track.
One signed `.aab`: Play generates per-device APKs from it and serves them signed with the app signing key, while the upload key only authenticates the bundle that was sent.
Upload a bundle only when the app ships native libraries: a JavaScript-only React Native app can still ship a signed APK.
mcqs.explanation: Google Play uses Android App Bundles to generate and deliver APKs optimized for each device configuration, so you build, sign and upload a single bundle instead of every ABI, density and locale combination; with Play App Signing the delivery APKs are signed with the app signing key, and the upload key is what authenticates the bundle you sent (https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9859152). The strongest distractor is option 0, because it sounds like the same optimization: with an APK the splitting decision would still have to be made, but Play does not repack an APK it receives - the per-device split is derived from the bundle's modules and manifest, which is why the artifact type is part of the submission format and not a packaging preference. Option 1 inverts the signing chain: the bundle you upload is signed with the upload key, and Play re-signs the generated APKs. Option 3 invents a scope rule: the bundle is the submission format for app releases regardless of whether the project has native code.

mcqs.question: A web developer ports a card component to React Native: a CSS grid rule, `1rem` padding, a `fontSize` declared on the wrapping container, and a `.card--active` modifier class toggled by state. Which statement describes what React Native actually supports?
options: `StyleSheet.create` turns the objects into scoped, CSS-like rules, so the `.card--active` modifier resolves by name instead of by array position.
Typography and color declared on a parent `<View>` inherit into nested `<Text>` elements, so the container-level font size keeps working after the port.
Styles are plain objects merged left to right on the `style` prop: there are no selectors or cascade, `flexDirection` defaults to `column`, and numeric sizes are density-independent pixels.
Percentage widths resolve against the device screen, so `width: '50%'` behaves like CSS `50vw` on every phone.
mcqs.explanation: React Native styles are JavaScript objects passed through the `style` prop; arrays merge left to right with later entries winning, so the modifier is just a second object in the array, and `flexDirection` defaults to `column` instead of CSS's `row` (https://reactnative.dev/docs/style, https://reactnative.dev/docs/flexbox). The strongest distractor is option 0: `StyleSheet.create` looks like the CSS-modules entry point, but it registers styles and returns them; it creates no scopes and no class names, so nothing is ever resolved by name. Option 1 imports CSS inheritance, but text styles inherit only from a `<Text>` ancestor, not from a `<View>`. Option 3 is the reverse of the documented rule: percentages resolve against the parent's size, not the screen.

mcqs.question: Deep links open the right screen while the app is running, but the same URL tapped from a cold start leaves the app on the initial route. The code registers `Linking.addEventListener('url', handler)` inside a component effect and navigates from that handler. What is the actual gap?
options: The listener subscribes too late: registering it before `AppRegistry.registerComponent` makes React Native replay the initial URL as a normal event.
The OS strips query parameters from the URL during a cold start, so the handler receives a link it cannot match and ignores it.
A cold start needs its own prefix, for example `example-cold://`, because the normal scheme is only registered once the app has already run.

A cold start delivers the URL once as the initial URL, which the listener never sees because it is not a `url` event; that path must be read and turned into navigation state, or delegated to `NavigationContainer`'s `linking`, which handles both entry points.
mcqs.explanation: Deep linking has two entry points: the initial URL that launched the app and the URL events that arrive while it runs. `NavigationContainer` with `linking` covers both; a hand-rolled solution has to call `Linking.getInitialURL()` in addition to subscribing (https://reactnavigation.org/docs/deep-linking). The strongest distractor is option 0: it notices the real symptom, that the subscription happens after the URL already arrived, but proposes a mechanism that does not exist. No registration order turns the launch URL into an event; it is a separate source, and moving `addEventListener` earlier leaves the cold start just as broken. Option 1 invents parameter stripping, since the platform hands over the full URL. Option 2 invents a second scheme; the custom scheme is declared once in the native configuration, not per launch mode.

mcqs.question: A progress bar animates `width` through `Animated.timing` and stutters whenever the JS thread is busy. A teammate changes the config to `useNativeDriver: true` and the bar stops animating, with React Native reporting that the style property is not supported by the native animated module. What is the correct reading?
options: Interpolate the value into the width output range and keep `useNativeDriver: true`: interpolation math runs on the native side, so the layout property becomes native-driven too.

The native driver only animates non-layout properties such as `opacity` and `transform`; a bar driven by `width` needs the JS driver, a `transform: [{ scaleX }]` rewrite, or a UI-thread style if the JS thread must stay free.
Set `isInteraction: false` on the animation: layout properties are only excluded from the native driver while the animation holds an interaction handle.
It is a development-only guard; a release build lets the native driver animate every style property.
mcqs.explanation: The native driver sends the whole animation to native before it starts, so it runs without the JS thread and without driving layout: you can animate non-layout properties such as `transform` and `opacity`, not flexbox or position properties (https://reactnative.dev/docs/animations). The strongest distractor is option 0 because it is half right: interpolation does execute natively for supported values, which makes the reasoning sound convincing, but the limit is the property the animation finally writes, not where the interpolation runs, and `width` stays a layout property. Option 2 confuses `isInteraction`, which controls whether the animation registers an interaction handle so lists can defer work, with driver support. Option 3 invents a build-mode gate that does not exist.

mcqs.question: Only low-end Android users report dropped frames while scrolling the feed. A React Native DevTools performance trace shows the JS thread mostly idle and short React commits during the scroll, while the in-app Perf Monitor FPS number still drops. What is the correct next step?
options: Take it to the platform profiler (Android Studio Profiler or a Perfetto system trace) on a physical device with a release-like build, because JS-idle jank is layout, drawing, image or view-count work that DevTools cannot attribute.
Throttle the CPU in DevTools and re-read the JS flame chart: a high enough multiplier turns a laptop into the low-end device and reproduces the dropped frames.
Memoize the rows and raise `windowSize`, because an idle JS thread means React work is still happening outside the profiler's sampling window.
Use the Perf Monitor FPS reading as the release measurement, since it renders the same JavaScript bundle users run.
mcqs.explanation: The debugging split is by substrate: DevTools covers JavaScript concerns such as console, breakpoints, component inspection, the React Profiler, network events, performance traces and memory snapshots, while frame cost on the native side belongs to the platform profilers, and jank should be reproduced on a physical device with Development Mode off (https://reactnative.dev/docs/debugging, https://reactnative.dev/docs/profiling). The strongest distractor is option 1: CPU throttling is a legitimate lab technique, but throttling the JS thread cannot attribute work that the trace already places outside the JS thread, and a dev build's extra instrumentation changes what is being measured. Option 2 prescribes JS-side fixes for a JS-idle profile, and raising `windowSize` mounts more rows. Option 3 promotes a diagnostic overlay into a measurement.

scenarios.prompt: Two bugs are reported against this chat list. (1) Tapping a row changes the parent's selection - the header counter proves it - but no row ever picks up the highlight; the highlight only appears after that same message is edited. (2) After a fast scroll the list shows blank bands where rows should be, and `scrollToIndex` for "jump to message" lands two or three messages away from the target. Message bodies wrap to two or three lines. Explain both bugs and rewrite the component.
rubric: Names the `memo` comparator as the selection bug: it never compares `selected`, so `memo` returns true and the row keeps its stale style while the parent state changes.
Separates that from `extraData`: the list already re-renders because `renderItem` changes with `selectedId`, so `extraData` is not the fix (and is only needed for a stable `renderItem`).
Explains the second symptom as `getItemLayout`'s fixed-geometry contract being violated by wrapped bodies, and either removes it or makes the height real with a clamped body.
Connects the wrong offsets to the observable effects: drifted virtualization window (blank bands) and `scrollToIndex` landing off by rows.
Proposes a verification plan on a representative device - fast scroll, index scroll to a wrapped message, render counts per row - instead of declaring the fix from the code.

scenarios.prompt: A teammate flipped `useNativeDriver` from `false` to `true` to fix a stuttering progress bar. Now the bar never animates and React Native reports that the style property is not supported by the native animated module. The `addListener`-to-`setState` wiring is still there, `progress` is a 0-1 fraction, and the component can unmount mid-animation. Predict what happens in each case, explain why, and rewrite the component so its frames no longer depend on the JS thread.
rubric: Predicts failure at start, not slow frames: the animation never begins because `width` (including its interpolation to a percentage) is a layout property the native driver cannot run.
Identifies the per-frame `setState` listener as the stutter in the JS-driver build, and explains that a React commit per frame ties the bar to JS-thread availability.
Rewrites with a non-layout property (`transform: [{ scaleX }]`) on the native driver, or a UI-thread style for the width case, and removes the listener from the render path.
Cleans up the animation and listener on unmount and on `progress` changes, and keeps one driver per `Animated.Value`.
States a verification method - JS deliberately blocked, profile on a physical release-like build - and keeps business and accessibility state on JS instead of per frame.

scenarios.prompt: Marketing sends two links: `example://feed` and `https://app.example.com/users/42`. The first opens the app but lands on Home instead of the Feed tab; the second opens the browser. The linking config below is the entire JavaScript-side setup. Explain both failures, rewrite the contract, and list what has to change outside the JavaScript bundle for the https link to reach the app.
rubric: Names the nesting mismatch as the cause of the Home landing: `Feed` sits inside `Home`, so the URL matches no screen and the container falls back to its initial route; the fix mirrors the tree and adds a wildcard.

Separates the two https failures: the missing prefix is a JavaScript parsing gap, while the domain association (Associated Domains and AASA on iOS, autoVerify and Digital Asset Links on Android) is decided by the OS before JS runs.
Treats URL parameters as untrusted input: validates `:id` before fetching and types the param list.
Keeps a single deep-link owner so cold start and foreground events do not double-navigate, using the `getInitialURL`/`subscribe` overrides when other sources exist.
Describes verification on both platforms including a cold start, and states the installed-app limit of universal links.
